SKM-SPN-0001.name: Sciatica / Lumbosacral Radicular Syndrome
SKM-SPN-0001.oneLine: Leg-dominant neural pain from lumbosacral nerve-root irritation/compression; diagnose clinically first, image when it answers a management or red-flag question.
definition: Sciatica is a clinical syndrome of radiating leg pain of neural origin arising from a lumbosacral nerve-root disorder.
Radicular pain means pain generated by root irritation; radiculopathy means objective neurological dysfunction such as weakness, sensory loss or reflex change.
Pain commonly travels below the knee and may coexist with paresthesia, numbness, weakness or foot drop.

anatomy.relevance: Most commonly implicated lower-lumbar levels in classic L5/S1 radicular syndromes.
Posterolateral disc herniation is common because lateral PLL reinforcement is limited.
Paracentral herniation typically compresses the traversing root.
Foraminal/far-lateral lesions typically affect the exiting root.
Highly pain-sensitive; foraminal compression can produce intense radicular pain.
Peripheral sciatic neuropathy can mimic root disease; exam pattern differentiates.

epidemiology.data: ~1.2–43% across studies because definitions/populations vary widely.
epidemiology.interpretation: Do not quote one universal prevalence.

epidemiology.data: Older literature suggests ~5–10% of low-back-pain patients have sciatica.
Lumbar disc herniation causes most classic sciatica; systematic reviews often cite ~85–90%.
epidemiology.interpretation: Stenosis and non-spinal mimics remain important.

epidemiology.data: WHO: low-back pain affected ~619 million people in 2020.
No single robust India-wide sciatica prevalence figure established.
epidemiology.interpretation: Use local/state/occupation studies only as local estimates.

riskGroups: Working-age/middle-aged adults are common in disc-related sciatica; degenerative stenotic radicular syndromes increase with age.
Whole-body vibration, repeated heavy lifting and awkward sustained loading can increase occupational risk in selected populations.
Drivers/heavy-equipment operators merit attention because vehicle vibration has been reported as a risk factor.
Smoking, obesity/metabolic health, previous episodes and psychosocial work stress may modify risk/recovery.
Sex association is inconsistent; avoid a fixed male:female ratio without a population-specific source.

pathophysiology.detail: Disc material, osteophyte, facet hypertrophy, spondylolisthesis or stenosis narrows root space.
Nucleus-pulposus exposure can trigger inflammatory mediators; pain may exceed visible compression.
Severe foraminal/canal compromise can impair root microcirculation.
DRG/root irritation causes electric pain, paresthesia and allodynia.
More significant root dysfunction causes objective myotomal weakness, reflex loss and possibly atrophy.

historyChecklist: Exact pain map: back → buttock → thigh → leg → foot/toes; is leg pain worse than back pain?
Tingling, numbness, objective sensory loss, weakness, foot slap/drop.
Bladder retention/incontinence, bowel dysfunction, saddle/genital numbness.
Fever, infection risk, cancer, weight loss, night pain, immunosuppression.
Occupation: lifting, driving/vibration, prolonged sitting, repetitive bending.
Previous episodes, MRI, injections/surgery and response.
NSAID/medicine safety: CKD, GI bleed, CVD, anticoagulants, pregnancy, allergies.

slrDegrees.interpretation: May reflect marked irritability but is nonspecific; recheck technique and consider hip/non-neural causes.
slrDegrees.action: Do not call severe disc prolapse from angle alone.

L4–5 paracentral → traversing L5; L5–S1 far-lateral → exiting L5
rootLocalization.function: Heel-walk difficulty, toe drag, foot drop

Buttock-dominant symptoms, nonconcordant lumbar root imaging, local provocative findings.
Groin pain, restricted internal rotation, hip provocative tests.
Provocation cluster; objective root deficit absent.
Exertional, less posture dependent; pulses/ABI abnormal.
Length-dependent bilateral sensory loss and distal reflex change.
Pure sensory lateral-thigh symptoms; no motor/reflex deficit.
Bladder/bowel/saddle dysfunction or major bilateral deficit — emergency.

Bilateral neuropathic symptoms, macrocytosis or deficiency risk
labs.why: Treatable neuropathy; not routine unilateral radiculopathy.

imagingTimeline.why: Imaging rarely changes early care and incidental degeneration is common.

imagingTimeline.why: Confirm concordant disc/root pathology for injection/surgery planning.

imagingTimeline.when: Objective progressive motor deficit / acute foot drop
imagingTimeline.why: Neurological progression matters more than pain score.

Spondylosis; may contribute to foraminal narrowing.
Can contribute to lateral recess/foraminal stenosis.
May contribute to central/foraminal stenosis; standing lateral useful.
Structural or pain-related posture; correlate clinically.
Changes pathway; may require urgent further imaging.
Does NOT exclude disc herniation/root compression.

mri.meaning: May be incidental; correlate with recess/foramen/root.
Focal herniation; clinical relevance depends on root contact/compression.
More extended herniation; often more likely to resorb than contained protrusion.
Free fragment; can migrate and cause acute severe radiculopathy.
More relevant to claudication/multiroot symptoms than isolated root pain.
Most valuable when level/side matches exam.

Selected alternative when MRI contraindicated/nondiagnostic; invasive.

treatmentTimeline.plan: Education, stay active within tolerance, short symptom-control medicine if appropriate, early symptom-guided rehab; avoid prolonged bed rest.
Progress rehab; repeat neurological examination; worsening motor deficit → earlier MRI/referral.
MRI if management will change; consider specialist pathway, selected epidural injection or surgical opinion.
Reassess diagnosis, conditioning, work exposure, smoking/metabolic health, psychosocial barriers; avoid chronic medication harm.

pharmacology.examples: Ibuprofen, diclofenac; selected COX-2 agent such as etoricoxib depending label/risk
pharmacology.evidence: Guidelines allow cautious short-duration use; sciatica-specific benefit is limited/uncertain.
pharmacology.cautions: GI, renal, BP/CV, anticoagulants, pregnancy, allergy; one NSAID at a time.

pharmacology.evidence: NICE does not recommend paracetamol alone for low-back pain.
Pregabalin RCT negative; NICE advises against gabapentinoids for sciatica.
pharmacology.cautions: Sedation, dizziness, edema, misuse/dependence, renal dosing.

pharmacology.evidence: Trial: modest function improvement but no meaningful pain benefit; NICE advises against.
pharmacology.cautions: Glucose, infection, mood, GI, bone risks.

pharmacology.role: Only if meaningful acute spasm coexists
pharmacology.evidence: Evidence pertains more to acute non-radicular LBP than true sciatica.

pharmacology.role: Avoid routine use; avoid chronic sciatica use

pharmacology.evidence: Does not decompress a nerve root.

interventions.when: Selected acute severe sciatica after specialist assessment
interventions.limit: Short-term benefit; not emergency decompression substitute.

interventions.when: Persistent disabling concordant radiculopathy despite reasonable conservative care, or earlier for significant/progressive deficit
interventions.limit: Faster relief in selected patients; long-term difference narrows.

Not routine after primary discectomy; selected instability/structural indication

surgeryDecision.criteria: No CES, no major/progressive motor deficit, tolerable symptoms, improving trajectory
surgeryDecision.action: Education + activity + rehab + limited symptom medication.

surgeryDecision.criteria: Objective weakness, foot drop, progressive sensory/motor loss, major functional loss
Persistent disabling radicular pain usually ~6–12 weeks, imaging concordant, non-surgical care unsuccessful
CES or rapidly progressive major neurological deficit
surgeryDecision.action: Urgent MRI and emergency surgical assessment.

prognosis: Most acute disc-related sciatica improves with time and conservative management.
Spontaneous disc resorption is common, especially extruded/sequestered fragments; WFNS cites roughly two-thirds overall in reviewed literature.
A substantial minority has persistent symptoms at 12 months; estimates vary by definition/population.
Surgery generally provides faster relief in selected surgical candidates; long-term differences versus non-surgical care diminish.
Poorer recovery can be associated with severe baseline disability, prolonged symptoms, work/psychosocial barriers, smoking, metabolic comorbidity and persistent neurological deficit.

lifestyle.why: Deconditioning and delayed functional recovery; staying active usually improves outcomes.

lifestyle.advice: Temporarily reduce repeated heavy lifting/twisting in high irritability
lifestyle.why: Reduces repeated provocation while graded recovery begins.
Associated with poorer spinal/disc and surgical outcomes.
Reduces comorbidity/mechanical burden; weight alone is not the diagnosis.
Food does not mechanically decompress a root; target diabetes, deficiency or bone-health indications specifically.

recall: Pain + dermatomal sensory change + myotomal weakness/reflex change localizes better than pain alone.
L4–5 paracentral → traversing L5. L5–S1 paracentral → traversing S1.
Heel walk = dorsiflexor/L5-predominant screen; toe walk/heel rise = S1.
SLR is sensitive; crossed SLR is more specific.
X-ray cannot directly show disc herniation.
MRI is ordered because it can change management—not because pain feels severe.
Pregabalin/gabapentin are neuropathic-pain drugs but are not guideline-supported routine sciatica drugs.
Conservative first unless CES, significant/progressive motor deficit or serious alternate pathology changes urgency.
